newsitem.title: UK: Three freed in Britain after 18 years in prison.
newsitem.headline: Three freed in Britain after 18 years in prison.

text.p: Three men jailed 18 years ago for the murder of a newspaper delivery boy walked free on Friday, in a case which delivered another body blow to the reputation of the British justice system.

Michael Hickey, his cousin Vincent Hickey, and James Robinson had consistently protested their innocence since being sentenced to life imprisonment in 1979 for the murder of 13-year-old Carl Bridgewater, shot dead during a burglary.
After two hours of legal representation, the three were released on unconditional bail pending an appeal on April 8.
They left the court arm in arm with ecstatic relatives, many of them in tears. Scores of well-wishers cheered, whistled and clapped as they appeared on the steps of London's High Court.
"It is the best feeling in the world. I am relieved. I would like to say how grateful we are to all those who helped us, the people who have believed in our innocence," said Vincent Hickey.
Theresa Robinson, a solicitor's secretary who married Robinson while he was in prison, punched the air with joy and wept openly after the bail decision was announced.
Robinson said he thought he was "tripping" when he had heard on Thursday night of his suddenly arranged court appearance.

Lawyers representing the men said police had tricked a fourth person, Patrick Molloy, into signing a confession after they said that Vincent Hickey had confessed. The lawyers said the Hickey confession was fabricated by police officers.

"It is only a small part of serious substantial and widespread police malpractice involving a number of very high-ranking officers down to the lowest rank who must have been involved in what was going on," said lawyer Michael Mansfield.

The convictions of the four were based on the confession from Molloy, who died in prison in 1981 after being convicted of manslaughter. Prosecution lawyers said they accepted the trial was fundamentally flawed and the convictions were unsafe.
"His (Molloy's) conviction must be regarded as unsafe," said prosecution lawyer Jeremy Roberts. It was recommended at their trial that all three should serve 25 years in jail.

The men, who had an appeal turned down by judges in 1989, staged rooftop protests in prison to profess their innocence and their families had waged a lengthy, high-profile battle to have their convictions overturned.
Michael Hickey's mother, Ann Whelan, said the policemen responsible for her son's conviction should now take his place.

"I want the police officers that behaved badly to go to prison and match year by year, day by day, minute by minute and second by second of what they have done to my son, Jim Robinson, Vincent Hickey and don't let's forget Patrick Molloy. That will do me nicely," she told reporters outside the court.
"My lad and the other two are leaving a cell today and I want the person that committed this crime to go in it."
Prime Minister John Major said he was sure there would be an inquiry into the original convictions.
The trio's release is the latest in a number of wrongful imprisonment cases in Britain that date back to the 1970s. Many involved Irishmen suspected of Irish Republican Army attacks.
In 1989, the so-called "Guildford Four" were released after convictions were quashed against them for a IRA bomb that killed five people in a pub.
In 1991, the "Birmingham Six" were freed after being cleared of 1974 pub bomb blasts that killed 21 people and injured 162.
The three could be entitled to compensation that may top two million pounds ($3.23 million).

Home secretary (Interior Minister) Michael Howard, himself a lawyer, said it was inevitable some mistakes would be made. "There is no such thing as an infallible system of human justice," he told BBC Television.
